newsitem.title: USA: U.S. soybean exports back on track as prices fall.
newsitem.headline: U.S. soybean exports back on track as prices fall.

text.p: U.S. export opportunities for soybeans are growing after a quick $2.00 per bushel price drop from springtime highs, oilseeds analysts said.

"I think what's happened is that the Brazilian basis has firmed up and our price has dropped which makes us competitive from August 1 forward," said Roy Huckabay, vice-president of LIT Investor Services.
U.S. exports tapered off in May and June after prices at the Chicago Board of Trade topped the $9.00 per bushel mark for the first time in 8-1/2 years.

Meanwhile, Brazilian exporters were shipping out a record crop at a large discount to U.S. prices. But Chicago Board of Trade futures fell nearly $2 a bushel in two months while Brazilian prices rose.

Rumors swirled recently at the CBOT that a cargo of U.S. old crop soybeans was sold from the U.S. Gulf for August shipment. U.S. exporters could not confirm the rumor but some said prices were conducive for an August sale.
The rumor sparked double-digit gains in morning trade Thursday. At 1207 CDT, soybeans were up 14-1/4 to 3-1/2 cents per bushel with August up 14-1/4 at $6.84-1/2.

Export prices at the U.S. Gulf have tumbled in recent days. CIF basis offers were down 20 cents a bushel on Thursday. That fall, coupled with Wednesday's 11 cent drop in CBOT futures, put the one-day flat price decline at 31 cents.

Trade sources quoted U.S. FOB Gulf soybean prices at $270.45 a tonne on Thursday. Brazilian beans FOB Paranagua were at $261.25 a tonne. Favorable freight prices would make U.S. supplies cheaper to some destinations, they said.
For September shipment, U.S. supplies were quoted at $235.43 a tonne, compared with $265.65 out of Brazil.

But Brazil has already registered 8.2 million tonnes of soybeans for export as of June 30 and may not have much left to sell, according to the Brazilian Association of Vegetable Oils Industries (Abiove).
In a report released Wednesday, Abiove said those registrations totalled roughly 92 percent of the total amount available for export.

"South American export premiums when you get into those deferred months are quite a bit higher than they were," said Mario Balletto, oilseeds analyst with Merrill Lynch. "They don't have the supplies there. From that standpoint we're getting very close to being competitive."
Independent consultants Safras e Mercado projected Brazil's February-June soybean exports would total 4.8 million tonnes, compared with 2.4 million for that period last year.
"Brazil is pretty much cleaned out," a veteran CBOT trader said. "They're not going to have much of anything for August. If anyone needs coverage then, they'll have to come to us."
